blocks.text: Single column validation, covered in the sibling Data Validation topic, asks whether any one column individually looks valid. Integrity is a different question: whether different parts of a dataset, or different tables, remain logically consistent with each other.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Type","What it requires","Example"],"rows":[["Entity integrity","Every row is uniquely identifiable, primary key never null or duplicated","Every customer_id is unique and never blank"],["Referential integrity","A foreign key value must exist in the table it references","Every order's customer_id corresponds to a real row in customers"],["Domain integrity","Every value comes from the actual set of valid values for that column","A status column contains only pending, shipped, or cancelled, never a typo like shpped"]]}

orders = pd.DataFrame({'order_id': [1,2,3,4], 'customer_id': [10, 11, 99, 10]})
customers = pd.DataFrame({'customer_id': [10, 11, 12]})

orphaned = orders[~orders['customer_id'].isin(customers['customer_id'])]
print(orphaned)
#    order_id  customer_id
# 2         3           99   <- references a customer that does not exist

has_duplicates = customers['customer_id'].duplicated().any()
has_nulls = customers['customer_id'].isna().any()
is_valid_key = not has_duplicates and not has_nulls   # BOTH conditions required

blocks.text: A valid primary key requires zero duplicates AND zero nulls, not just one of the two conditions.

blocks.text: 5. Why Integrity Problems Surface After a Merge

A merge combining two previously separately clean tables can reveal they were never actually consistent with each other. This is often the first time an integrity problem becomes visible, since each table looked fine in isolation.

code.content:
merged = orders.merge(customers, on='customer_id', how='left')
missing = merged[merged['customer_id'].isna() == False]  # rows with a customer_id that did not match
unmatched_count = orders.shape[0] - orders['customer_id'].isin(customers['customer_id']).sum()
print(f"{unmatched_count} orders reference a customer that does not exist")

items: Validating each table individually and assuming that guarantees correctness across tables, integrity specifically requires checking the RELATIONSHIPS between tables, not just each one in isolation.
Only checking integrity once at the start of a project rather than treating it as an ongoing property that a growing dataset can violate over time.
Verify every primary key column has zero duplicates and zero nulls.
Check every foreign key against the table it references using isin().
Compare actual unique values in categorical columns against the explicitly allowed set.
Re-run integrity checks after every merge or join, not just before.
Treat integrity as an ongoing property, not a one time audit.
